units.unit: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units
tenants are poor with no bargaining power so landlords can raise rents freely
living conditions are unsafe and crowded and affordable alternatives are scarce
a rent cap can be paired with safety rules to protect people rather than just cutting supply
if landlords must meet safety rules they need some money back
the cap should be high enough to allow that but still stop sudden big rises
the shakier half is that a cap stops big rises
wants a source on a Hong Kong case where a cap played out
wants a counter-view that caps make landlords leave or cut supply
D6 is a model of whether caps cut supply with Hong Kong-like cases
D2 is actual rent data to check if rises happened
D5 is the landlords' counter-view
the existing Hong Kong rule only limits rises inside a tenancy
stock kept growing so a moderate tightening looks safe
a hard cap on starting rent looks risky
rents rose faster than general rents and burden got worse so the current rule is not enough
the landlords' evidence is weak
a binding hard cap would hurt the people it is meant to help so would not do that
tighten the second-generation type by lowering the allowed rise inside tenancies
make the rule cover small tenancies too since reporting is voluntary below the threshold
that keeps protection without forcing exits
needs to know if tenants actually gain
tenant gain means longer tenancies and fewer forced moves
plus rents that stay affordable relative to income
D8 is a second-generation scheme over the long run which is the type favoured
D3 is a real tenant's view on insecurity
D11 surveys tenants on tenure security which is the measure of gain
still says tighten but the tightening should be about security of tenure and the tenancy rise limit not rent levels
tenants care more about the queue and not being thrown out than about cheaper rent
New York shows a cost: less upkeep and fewer listings after tightening
picks claim, evidence, objection, reply because the position is refined and must be defended
the main task is to defend against the supply-loss objection from D6 and the landlords
the objection carries both D6 supply loss and the D8 upkeep and listing cost
the landlords' weak evidence goes in the reply as a reason not to take their exit threat at full face value
still accepts the risk is real
it would need to show the threat is real but manageable
for example that inspection and tenure rules can be enforced cheaply
D9 is a legal opinion on compensation risk that tests whether the tightening is legally manageable
skipping D10 because it is marked draft and not for circulation so should not be relied on in an essay
D9 supports the refined view
a hard cap on starting rent risks compensation claims while rules on tenancy terms are on firmer ground
a light band could be a later step but needs survey data that does not exist yet
recommend tenure security and a tighter rise limit first and a band only after data is built
